overview: Yakama communities belong to the Columbia Plateau of present-day Washington. The map’s Yakima and Yakama labels show differently sized regional outlines, not the boundaries of a single ancient state. The fourteen tribes and bands confederated under the 1855 treaty had distinct earlier identities. This card follows Yakama history into that later nation; its institutions should not be projected into the map’s 1492 or 1530 scenes.

periods.title: Communities and seasonal homelands
periods.summary: Families moved among fishing places, root grounds, mountain gathering areas and winter villages.

periods.title: Treaty and reservation
periods.summary: The 1855 agreement established a confederation and reservation while reserving fishing and gathering rights.

periods.title: Nation and renewal
periods.summary: Tribal government and cultural renewal continue.

items.text: Before Fort Simcoe became the first formal Yakama agency in 1859, the place was Mool-mool, a seasonal camp with bubbling spring water. Families stopped there while hunting, fishing, gathering roots and picking huckleberries. A later military and administrative location had an older life as a busy food-gathering crossroads.

Chief Kamiakin’s garden in the Upper Ahtanum Valley grew corn, peas, potatoes, squash, melons and wheat before the 1855 war. A ditch about a quarter-mile long brought water to it. Gardening was part of his community’s changing economy alongside seasonal fishing and gathering.

Signed on June 9, 1855, the treaty named fourteen tribes and bands as a confederated nation and ceded extensive lands to the United States. It set aside a reservation. Ratification followed in March 1859, nearly four years after the signing.

War followed in 1855 amid settler encroachment and killings. Kamiakin helped lead resistance, and his forces initially drove back an American military expedition. Colonel George Wright’s 1858 campaign broke organized resistance. Kamiakin stayed away from the reservation and eventually lived at Rock Lake.

The treaty’s practical details reach right into family life. Article 3 reserved fishing at customary places and hunting and gathering on open, unclaimed land. Article 5 promised schools, a hospital, medicines and a physician. These were written government commitments, not proof that every promised service arrived.

The tribal council formally established in 1944 has fourteen members, recalling the treaty’s fourteen signers. The museum describes a General Council of adult members electing representatives by raised hands. The nation officially adopted the spelling Yakama in 1994; older records commonly say Yakima.

The seasonal round was a moving food calendar. A historical reconstruction describes spring root digging, summer fishing and travel to cooler high ground, followed by mountain huckleberry gathering. Knowledge of when different foods were ready helped families use several landscapes across the year.

Winter brought families back to sheltered valley camps with stored roots, berries, salmon and venison. People repaired homes, made tools and clothing, and visited one another. The pantry had been assembled over many months; winter preparation involved much more than one enormous shopping trip.

In a 1995 cultural-resources memorandum, Florence Aguilar explained meals beginning with water, followed by salmon, deer or elk, roots and berries, and ending with water. Her account connects eating with gratitude and responsibility for the waters that sustain salmon.

A Yakama basket in the National Museum of the American Indian combines cedar roots, beargrass, sedge and hide thong. Its maker used coiling and imbricated decoration, layering materials into a patterned surface. The museum received it in 1957, but does not know its maker or manufacture date.

At the intertribal fishery of Celilo Falls, Yakama and other fishers worked from platforms above dangerous currents. Raymond Matheny’s 1952 notes describe long-handled nets and compulsory safety ropes. Some fishers worked in groups and divided the proceeds from the fish they sold.

On March 10, 1957, water backed up behind The Dalles Dam and submerged Celilo Falls. The government paid compensation for flooded fishing sites, but did not buy away treaty fishing rights. Losing the falls damaged a place of work, trade, family memory and ceremony.

A small written sample of modern Ichishkíin is “Shix̱ iwá wyáx̱ayx̱t”, translated “Life is Good”. It appears as a storybook title on the Yakama language program’s page, credited to the Northwest Indian Language Institute and recorded by the nation’s program. This is contemporary teaching material.

Language lessons can accompany the busiest moments of parenting. The Yakama program offers resources for nursing, babyboards and diapering through meet-ups with Ttáwax̱t Birth Justice Center. Its handwashing poster and video bring language into hygiene routines too. Even changing a diaper can have vocabulary practice attached.

The nation’s 2017 coho restoration plan reported fish returning to Wenatchee and Methow watersheds and reproducing naturally. It also reported that local broodstock had replaced reliance on transfers from the lower Columbia. Building self-sustaining populations remained a long-term project, with monitoring as well as hatchery work.

ending.text: The imported map cutoffs do not mark the disappearance of Yakama people. The later nation continues through its government and treaty relationship, while language programs help families carry Ichishkíin into everyday life.
